To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the quality of breast cancer care in the Netherlands has improved over the last decade, (ii) there is substantial variation in care quality between hospitals, (iii) the rankability of hospitals is sensitive to case-mix and random variation, (iv) the rankability is improved by using a risk-adjustment method, (v) the improvement in rankability is larger when the risk-adjustment method is based on more than one indicator.

the quality of breast cancer care in Canada is high, that there is substantial variability in the quality of care between hospitals, that the variation is not explained by case mix, that there are no significant differences in quality of care between the 10 provinces/territories, and that there is no association between quality of care and the number of cases of breast cancer treated by each hospital.

the effect of random variation on breast cancer care quality indicators is substantial, that case-mix adjustment reduces random variation, that the effect of case-mix adjustment on the quality of breast cancer care is substantial and that the effect of the case-mix adjustment is not uniform across indicators, with some indicators being more sensitive to random variation than others.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How do we rank the quality of health care providers?
the following questions: (i) How does the random variation in the data affect the quality of the indicators and their ability to rank hospitals?
the following questions: 1) How does the quality of breast cancer care vary across hospitals and over time?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the case-mix adjusted quality indicators is recommended for the assessment of quality of breast cancer care, but that the case-mix adjustment should not be applied to all indicators.
there is no evidence to suggest that the use of a particular type of case mix adjustment method has any significant effect on the ranking of hospitals by quality of care.
the quality of care provided by the NHS is not good enough, and that the government and the NHS need to take steps to improve the quality of care that is provided to patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the effect of case-mix and random variation is substantial on the quality indicators of breast cancer care, and that it is possible to identify the indicators that are the least sensitive to random variation.
the effect of random variation is a significant confounder in the assessment of quality of breast cancer care, and that the magnitude of this effect varies across quality measures.
we developed and validated a new method for ranking the performance of health care providers on a set of quality indicators.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quality of care indicators used to rank hospitals for breast cancer care are not robust to random variation and case mix.
the use of breast cancer care quality indicators is not a reliable method for ranking hospitals.
the use of case-mix adjusted quality indicators in the context of a ranking exercise should be approached with caution.
